response: The function `is_not_prime` returns True when its input n is not a prime number and False when it is prime. It first handles the special case n == 1, which is not prime by definition, so it returns True immediately. For every other input, it loops over candidate divisors i from 2 up to the integer part of the square root of n, inclusive. If n is divisible by any of these i (that is, n % i equals 0), it has a nontrivial factor and the function returns True. If the loop finishes without finding a divisor, the function returns False. Checking only up to the square root is sufficient because any composite n must have a factor no greater than its square root. One caveat is that the function returns False for n = 0 and for negative numbers, since the loop range is empty or the modulus behaves unexpectedly, so it is really a test for composite numbers greater than 1 rather than a complete "not prime" check.
